  arise where host density is low enough for wind to disrupt the aggregation pheromone plume on

# Introduction

Disturbance refugia, defined by @krawchuk2020 as locations disturbed less severely or less frequently than the surrounding landscape, have become a organising concept for forest conservation under climate change. The concept is well developed for fire and much less so for insects. @krawchuk2020 note that few studies have explicitly identified refugia from insect outbreaks, and they propose a specific and testable mechanism for the most consequential insect disturbance in western North America. Refugia from mountain pine beetle (*Dendroctonus ponderosae* Hopkins), they suggest, could occur in areas of lower host density, where thinner stands allow greater wind penetration and so disrupt the aggregation pheromone communication on which mass attack depends.

The hypothesis is attractive because it is mechanistic and because each of its parts is independently plausible. Mass attack requires beetles to overwhelm host defences in a coordinated pulse, and the coordination is chemical. Beetle dispersal above the canopy is a flight behaviour sensitive to ambient conditions [@gray1972; @jones2019]. Thinner stands admit more wind. What has been missing is a spatial test.

@cartwright2018 came closest. Working at 30 m in lodgepole and whitebark pine in southern Oregon, she identified refugia from Landsat moisture anomalies during a 2009 drought and mountain pine beetle outbreak and modelled their landscape controls. Refugia were associated with topographically shaded slopes, convergent positions such as valleys, low soil bulk density, and thinner stands. The thinner-stand result is the host-density half of the hypothesis, confirmed. But she had no wind surface, so the mechanism itself went untested.

Testing it requires a wind surface, and that is where the problem starts. Gridded wind products of the kind now trivially available, the Global Wind Atlas among them, are produced by downscaling coarse mesoscale fields over a digital elevation model [@davis2023; @badger2014]. A wind surface built this way is in part a transform of the terrain it was draped over. Offered to a model alongside elevation it is not an independent measurement, and the severity of the dependence is a function of the analysis extent: a coarse driving field is nearly flat over a few kilometres, so at small extents almost all the variation in the product is terrain. An analyst working at the scale of a burn perimeter or a cluster of field plots, which is the scale at which most disturbance ecology is done, is in the worst position and has the least warning.

A second and more elementary trap attends refugia work specifically. A cell that was not attacked may hold no host. Under the @krawchuk2020 framing this is the difference between asking what a place is a refugium *from* and what it is a refugium *for*, and it cannot be resolved without an independent map of host abundance. The precedent here is old and pointed: @hadley1994 predicted heavier beetle mortality on hot, dry, south-facing slopes and found the reverse, because host density rather than moisture stress governed where attack succeeded.

We take these three problems to one landscape. We ask:

1.  Does terrain condition beetle-caused mortality once host abundance is accounted for, and where along the elevation gradient does host stop explaining the pattern?
2.  Does the component of the wind surface that is independent of elevation predict reduced attack where host is present, as @krawchuk2020 hypothesise?
3.  How much does the answer to question 2 depend on decisions the analyst makes freely: the extent of the study area, the grain of the cells, and whether damage is coded as a binary or as the ordinal severity class the survey records?

The design is built to make the third question answerable rather than rhetorical. The same response, the same predictors and the same model are refitted across each of those three axes: once across the full landscape and once inside a 2 by 4 km clip drawn from it, at 25 m, 50 m and 100 m, and at each severity threshold in turn. Two of the three change the answer, and they are not the two that get reported.

# Materials

## Study area

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the South Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. The terrain grid spans 16 by 17.5 km and **`r format(round(GRID_RELIEF), big.mark = ",")` m of relief**, from valley bottom to alpine. The modelled area is a subset of it, because cells carrying no inventory basal area cannot enter a model that conditions on stand structure; @tbl-relief reports the extent and relief of that subset, which are necessarily smaller. Both numbers are correct and they are not interchangeable. That range crosses the full biogeoclimatic sequence of the southern interior wet belt, from the dry warm Interior Cedar-Hemlock subzones through the moist warm subzones to the Engelmann Spruce-Subalpine Fir zone and its parkland variant [@ketcheson1991; @braumandl2005]. Lodgepole pine (*Pinus contorta* var. *latifolia*), the beetle's principal host here, occupies the middle of that sequence and is scarce at both ends.

The site description and the terrain surfaces are inherited from a companion analysis of conifer regeneration on the same ground [@murphy2026], which used them to predict seedling intensity after a 2015 mixed-severity wildfire. Disturbance was a predictor in that study. Here it is the response.

## Beetle-caused mortality

```{r}
#| label: read-response
#| echo: true

aos_box <- ext(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005"))
aos <- vect(here("02.inputs/aos/pest_infestation_poly.gdb"),
            layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = aos_box)
mpb <- project(aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM", ], crs(G))   # IBM = mountain pine beetle
m   <- mpb[mpb$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]

## BC severity classes are ordinal: trace, light, moderate, severe, very severe
sev_rank <- c(T = 1, L = 2, M = 3, S = 4, V = 5)
m$sev <- unname(sev_rank[m$PEST_SEVERITY_CODE]); m$sev[is.na(m$sev)] <- 0

severity  <- rasterize(m, G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)

c(polygons = nrow(m), years = length(unique(m$CAPTURE_YEAR)),
  hectares = round(sum(m$AREA_HA)))
```

The response is the British Columbia Aerial Overview Survey, the operational provincial record of forest health, in which observers sketch-map damage annually from fixed-wing aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species. We take polygons coded `IBM`, mountain pine beetle, for the outbreak window 1999 to 2015, and rasterise the maximum severity class reached by each cell.

Using the survey rather than a spectral classification is a deliberate trade. Red attack has been mapped from Landsat with respectable and improving accuracy [@white2005; @meddens2013; @ye2021], but every such product is a model whose errors are spatially structured and not independent of terrain, because illumination, shadow and view angle all vary with slope and aspect. For a question about terrain, a response generated by a terrain-sensitive classifier risks recovering the classifier's own terrain sensitivity. Sketch-mapping has larger and cruder errors, but they are observer errors, not errors generated by the predictors under test.

The severity scale is anchored to ground measurement. Twenty-eight field plots established in beetle-affected stands in 2020 recorded the basal area of pine killed, spanning 0.6 to 47.4 m2/ha, or 1.3 to 94.7 per cent of plot basal area, and these calibrated the spectral mapping used in the companion study [@murphy2026]. Plot coordinates were not recoverable from the project archive, so the plots calibrate the severity scale but cannot be used to check the spatial placement of individual survey polygons. We state that limit rather than implying a spatial validation we did not perform.

## Host abundance

```{r}
#| label: read-host
#| echo: true

vri <- project(vect(here("02.inputs/vri/vri_darkwoods.geojson")), crs(G))
vd  <- as.data.frame(vri)
num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))

## VRI records up to three species per polygon with percentage cover
accumulate <- function(pattern) {
  out <- rep(0, nrow(vd))
  for (i in 1:3) {
    cd <- vd[[paste0("SPECIES_CD_", i)]]
    pc <- num(vd[[paste0("SPECIES_PCT_", i)]]); pc[is.na(pc)] <- 0
    out <- out + ifelse(!is.na(cd) & grepl(pattern, cd), pc, 0)
  }
  out
}
vri$PinePct <- accumulate("^PL")               # lodgepole, the primary host
vri$Basal   <- num(vd$BASAL_AREA)

host <- rast(lapply(c("PinePct","Basal"), function(f) rasterize(vri, G, field = f)))
names(host) <- c("PinePct","Basal")
c(vri_polygons = nrow(vri), with_lodgepole = sum(vri$PinePct > 0))
```

Host abundance comes from the provincial Vegetation Resources Inventory, layer `VEG_COMP_LYR_R1_POLY`, retrieved from the British Columbia Data Catalogue web feature service for the study window. We accumulate the percentage cover of lodgepole pine across the three species slots each polygon records, and carry stand basal area alongside it.

The inventory's vintage matters and we state it. These polygons carry a reference year of 2014 and an interpretation date of August 2014, with an attribution base date of 1 January 2014; the projected date of 31 December 2025 is the growth model's roll-forward of age, height and volume, not a re-observation. Species composition therefore comes from photography flown in the fourteenth year of a seventeen-year outbreak window.

That is a limitation we cannot remove and should not hide. A stand whose pine was killed early in the outbreak will have been interpreted after the fact, and its recorded lodgepole percentage will be lower than the pine it carried when the beetle arrived. The bias runs in a specific direction: host is under-recorded exactly where attack was heaviest and earliest. It is therefore a candidate explanation for the reversal of the lodgepole coefficient at the severe threshold reported in @sec-ordinal, and we say so there rather than reading that reversal as ecology alone. It does not touch the presence-absence distinction the layer is mainly used for, since a stand that carried enough pine to be killed is not recorded as pine-free.

Without this layer the analysis cannot distinguish a refugium from an absence of pine, and that the distinction accounts for most of the apparent terrain signal.

## Terrain and wind

```{r}
#| label: read-terrain
#| echo: true

to_grid <- function(f) {
  r <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", f))
  b <- project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), crs(r))
  project(crop(r, b, snap = "out"), G, method = "bilinear")
}
terr <- rast(list(Elevation = G,               Slope = to_grid("Slope.utm.tif"),
                  TWI       = to_grid("TWI.utm.tif"),
                  RIX       = to_grid("Rutm.tif"),
                  Wind      = to_grid("Wind.utm.tif")))
names(terr) <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind")

## Topographic position: mean deviation from a surrounding annulus.
tpi <- function(r, w) {
  k <- matrix(1, w, w); k[ceiling(w/2), ceiling(w/2)] <- 0
  r - focal(r, k / sum(k), fun = sum, na.policy = "omit", na.rm = TRUE)
}
terr$TPI600 <- tpi(G, 25)     # ~625 m neighbourhood
```

```{r}
#| label: aspect-terms
#| echo: true

## Two surfaces built from aspect, which the inherited set lacks entirely.
## Both are computed directly from the elevation model rather than draped over
## it, which is why @tbl-orthogonality can show them independent of elevation.
d2r <- pi / 180
asp  <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Aspect.utm.tif"))
slp  <- rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Slope.utm.tif"))
stopifnot(identical(dim(asp), dim(G)), identical(as.vector(ext(asp)), as.vector(ext(G))))

## Heat load after McCune and Keon, aspect folded about the SW-NE axis so that
## southwest is hottest. Flat cells carry a -1 sentinel; the sin(slope) factor
## nulls the aspect term there, so the substitution below is inert.
asp[asp < 0] <- 225
fold <- abs(180 - abs(asp - 225))
LAT  <- mean(crds(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:4326"))[, 2])
terr$HLI <- 0.339 + 0.808 * cos(LAT*d2r) * cos(slp*d2r) -
            0.196 * sin(LAT*d2r) * sin(slp*d2r) -
            0.482 * cos(fold*d2r) * sin(slp*d2r)

## Winstral shelter index: the maximum upwind slope angle within SEARCH metres
## along a bearing. Positive means terrain rises upwind, so the cell is
## sheltered; negative means it is exposed. The Global Wind Atlas gives speed
## but no direction, so rather than assume a prevailing bearing we compute all
## eight and average, giving an omnidirectional shelter index.
SEARCH <- 500
shift_mat <- function(m, dr, dc) {
  nr <- nrow(m); nc <- ncol(m); out <- matrix(NA_real_, nr, nc)
  ri <- seq_len(nr); ci <- seq_len(nc); sr <- ri + dr; sc <- ci + dc
  vr <- sr >= 1 & sr <= nr; vc <- sc >= 1 & sc <= nc
  out[ri[vr], ci[vc]] <- m[sr[vr], sc[vc]]
  out
}
zm <- as.matrix(G, wide = TRUE); rstep <- res(G)[1]
sx_dir <- function(az) {
  th <- az * d2r; best <- matrix(-Inf, nrow(zm), ncol(zm))
  for (k in 1:floor(SEARCH / rstep)) {
    dc <- round(k * sin(th)); dr <- round(-k * cos(th))
    if (dc == 0 && dr == 0) next
    best <- pmax(best, atan((shift_mat(zm, dr, dc) - zm) / (k * rstep)) / d2r, na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  best[!is.finite(best)] <- NA_real_
  best
}
sx <- rast(lapply(seq(0, 315, by = 45), function(a) {
  r <- G; values(r) <- as.vector(t(sx_dir(a))); r }))
terr$SxMean <- app(sx, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Terrain surfaces are inherited unchanged from @murphy2026, which derived them from the 1 m Natural Resources Canada High Resolution Digital Elevation Model [@nrcan2017], smoothed, depression-filled by the algorithm of @wang2006 and aggregated to 25 m, with compound indices following @beers1973 and @parker1982. We add three surfaces of our own. The first is a topographic position index at a 625 m neighbourhood, because @cartwright2018 found slope, elevation and heat load among the strongest controls on refugia and reported topographic position alongside them, and the inherited set carried no measure of topographic position at all.

The other two exist because the inherited set carries no aspect information at all, and so contains no term that can distinguish a warm slope from a cold one at the same elevation. That matters here specifically, because the confound this paper cannot resolve is between wind exposure and cold, and aspect bears on the two differently. We therefore compute a heat load index after @mccune2002, in which aspect is folded about the southwest to northeast axis so that southwest is hottest, and a shelter index after @winstral2002, the maximum upwind slope angle within 500 m along a bearing, which is positive where terrain rises upwind and negative on exposed convexities. The Global Wind Atlas supplies speed but no direction, so rather than assume a prevailing bearing we compute the shelter index on all eight cardinal and intercardinal bearings and average them, giving an omnidirectional index that requires no assumption about wind direction.

The decisive property of both is how they are built. They are derived from the elevation model by trigonometry rather than draped over it by downscaling, and @tbl-orthogonality shows the consequence: their variance is essentially unrelated to elevation, where the wind product's is largely elevation. A terrain-derived predictor is not automatically an elevation transform. The distinction is in the construction, not in the fact of using a digital elevation model.

The ruggedness surface carries a documentation gap we state rather than paper over. Its exact formulation is not recorded beyond the citations above, and its distribution is inconsistent with a vector ruggedness measure. We treat it as a reproducible but unnamed ruggedness surface and confine claims to its statistical behaviour.

Ambient wind is Global Wind Atlas mean wind speed at 10 m above ground level [@globalwindatlas]. The atlas is built by driving a mesoscale model from reanalysis, generalising the result by the method of @badger2014 to remove the local terrain and roughness signal, and then downscaling it microscale over a digital elevation model and a land-cover roughness map [@davis2023]. Elevation and roughness are therefore inputs to the product, not covariates measured independently of it. That construction is why it cannot be assumed independent of elevation, and testing that assumption is the second half of this paper.

## Climate records

Because the interpretation in @sec-krawchuk turns on whether it is cold enough at the top of the gradient to kill beetles, we assembled the observational record that bears on it. Hourly observations from the British Columbia Wildfire Service network and daily observations from the Environment and Climate Change Canada network were retrieved for all stations within 100 km of the study area for the winters of the outbreak window. Retrieval is done by the script in `02.inputs/climate/`, which streams roughly 2.7 GB of hourly and daily observations and writes the per-station-winter summary the manuscript reads. That division is deliberate: the network fetch and the reduction of hourly series to winter summaries cannot sit inside a document render, but every decision about which records to believe is made in @sec-cold, in code, and is visible there.

Two screens matter. Many older Wildfire Service sensors floor at exactly -20.0 °C, so a station-winter whose minimum sits exactly on that floor has an unknown true minimum and is excluded; the rule is applied and checked in @sec-cold rather than inherited. Isolated single-observation spikes, colder than both neighbouring observations by more than 15 °C, are rejected as instrument error at the observation level, which is the one screen that must happen during retrieval because it needs the sub-daily series. One such value, a -40.0 °C daily minimum recorded on a day whose maximum was -4.5 °C and carrying no quality flag, would otherwise have produced exactly the conclusion the record does not support.

This network cannot furnish a temperature surface, for the reasons @sec-cold sets out. It can establish whether lethal temperatures occur in this region at all, which is a weaker claim and a sufficient one.

```{r}
#| label: assemble
#| echo: true

clip_src <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Oubteak.2005.tif"))
in_clip  <- rasterize(project(as.polygons(ext(clip_src), crs = crs(clip_src)), crs(G)),
                      G, field = 1, background = 0)

X <- as.data.frame(c(terr, host, severity, in_clip), na.rm = FALSE)
names(X)[(ncol(X) - 1):ncol(X)] <- c("Severity","InClip")
X$Attacked <- X$Severity > 0
X$HasHost  <- !is.na(X$PinePct) & X$PinePct > 0

## spatial blocks for resampling-based inference
rc <- rowColFromCell(G, seq_len(ncell(G)))
X$block <- paste(rc[,1] %/% BLOCK, rc[,2] %/% BLOCK, sep = "_")

PRED  <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind","TPI600")
EXTRA <- c("HLI","SxMean")          # aspect-derived; enter only the extended model
MVARS <- c(PRED, "PinePct", "Basal")   # defines the analysis frame, deliberately unchanged

## Cells lacking an inventory basal area are unmapped or non-productive and cannot
## enter a model that conditions on stand structure. Dropping them is reported here
## rather than left to silent na.action inside glm.
n_before <- sum(complete.cases(X[, PRED]) & !is.na(X$PinePct))
S <- X[complete.cases(X[, MVARS]), ]
H <- S[S$HasHost, ]
c(with_terrain_and_host = n_before, dropped_no_basal_area = n_before - nrow(S),
  analysis_cells = nrow(S), km2 = round(nrow(S) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6, 1),
  attacked = sum(S$Attacked), host_cells = nrow(H))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-relief
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The analysis landscape, and the 2 by 4 km clip drawn from it that the companion study used. The clip samples under two thirds of the relief and under 4 per cent of the cells."

tibble(
  Extent = c("full landscape", "2 by 4 km clip"),
  Cells  = c(nrow(S), sum(S$InClip == 1)),
  `Area (km²)` = round(c(nrow(S), sum(S$InClip == 1)) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6, 1),
  `Elevation (m)` = c(sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(S$Elevation), max(S$Elevation)),
                      sprintf("%.0f to %.0f", min(S$Elevation[S$InClip==1]),
                                              max(S$Elevation[S$InClip==1]))),
  `Relief (m)` = round(c(diff(range(S$Elevation)), diff(range(S$Elevation[S$InClip==1])))),
  `Attacked (%)` = round(100 * c(mean(S$Attacked), mean(S$Attacked[S$InClip==1])), 1)
) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrlrr", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11)
```

# Methods

## Inference

The response is heavily clustered, so cell counts vastly overstate independent information. All coefficients are accompanied by percentile intervals from a spatial block bootstrap in which the landscape is partitioned into blocks of `r BLOCK` by `r BLOCK` cells, roughly 1 km on a side, and blocks are resampled with replacement `r B_BOOT` times. Blocks of this size are larger than any plausible correlation range of the survey polygons. We report the point estimate, the block interval, and the proportion of resamples reproducing the sign of the point estimate, and we treat a term as supported only when the interval excludes zero.

```{r}
#| label: fn-boot
#| echo: true

## The bootstrap refits several hundred times on >100,000 rows, so it works on a
## model matrix built once and calls glm.fit directly. This is arithmetically
## identical to glm() with the same formula, and roughly thirty times faster.
MODEL_VARS <- c("Elevation","WindResid","PinePct","Basal","TPI600","Slope","TWI","RIX")

design_matrix <- function(z, vars = MODEL_VARS)
  cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1, as.matrix(z[, vars, drop = FALSE]))

fit_fast <- function(Xm, y) glm.fit(Xm, y, family = binomial())

block_boot <- function(z, vars = MODEL_VARS, B = B_BOOT, seed = 42) {
  Xm <- design_matrix(z, vars); y <- z$y
  idx_of <- split(seq_len(nrow(z)), z$block)
  blocks <- names(idx_of)
  set.seed(seed)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, B, ncol(Xm), dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Xm)))
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    idx <- unlist(idx_of[sample(blocks, length(blocks), replace = TRUE)], use.names = FALSE)
    f <- try(fit_fast(Xm[idx, , drop = FALSE], y[idx]), silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(f, "try-error")) out[b, ] <- coef(f)
  }
  out
}

model_table <- function(z, vars = MODEL_VARS, seed = 42) {
  Xm <- design_matrix(z, vars)
  fit <- fit_fast(Xm, z$y)
  cf  <- coef(fit)
  se  <- sqrt(diag(chol2inv(fit$qr$qr[1:fit$rank, 1:fit$rank, drop = FALSE])))
  bs  <- block_boot(z, vars, seed = seed)
  tibble(term = names(cf), beta = as.numeric(cf), naive_z = as.numeric(cf / se),
         lo = apply(bs, 2, quantile, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
         hi = apply(bs, 2, quantile, .975, na.rm = TRUE),
         sign_stab = sapply(names(cf), function(n)
                       mean(sign(bs[, n]) == sign(cf[n]), na.rm = TRUE)))
}

fmt_model <- function(mt) {
  mt |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    transmute(Term = term, beta = sprintf("%+.3f", beta),
              `naive z` = sprintf("%+.1f", naive_z),
              `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", lo, hi),
              `sign stability` = sprintf("%.2f", sign_stab),
              Supported = ifelse(lo * hi > 0, "yes", "no"))
}
```

## Orthogonalisation

Because the wind surface is built over the elevation surface, its coefficient in a model that also contains elevation is estimated from whatever small part of the joint distribution allows the two to vary separately. We therefore replace wind by the residual of wind regressed on elevation, rescaled to unit variance.

It is important to be exact about what this does and does not achieve, because it is easy to present it as a remedy for collinearity and it is not one. The substitution is a linear reparameterisation of the same model. Fitted values and deviance are unchanged, and by the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem the residualised coefficient is the raw wind coefficient multiplied by the square root of one minus the R² of wind on elevation, with its standard error scaled identically. The test statistic, and therefore every supported-or-not verdict in this paper, is numerically the same in both parameterisations. Orthogonalisation buys no precision whatever: the estimate still comes from the same narrow part of the joint distribution, and the variance inflation is untouched. What changes is the interpretation of the two coefficients. The wind coefficient now refers to the part of the wind surface that elevation does not explain, which is the quantity the @krawchuk2020 hypothesis is about, and the elevation coefficient becomes the total elevation association including whatever is transmitted through wind, rather than the partial effect at fixed wind. The reparameterisation is worth making for that reason alone, and for no other.

```{r}
#| label: design
#| echo: true

standardise <- function(dd) {
  vars <- intersect(c(PRED, EXTRA, "PinePct", "Basal"), names(dd))
  z <- as.data.frame(scale(dd[, vars]))
  z$y     <- as.integer(dd$Attacked)
  z$block <- dd$block
  z$Severity <- dd$Severity          # carried for the ordinal fits in @sec-ordinal
  z$WindResid <- as.numeric(scale(residuals(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = z))))
  z
}
Z  <- standardise(S)     # whole landscape
ZH <- standardise(H)     # cells containing lodgepole
ZC <- standardise(S[S$InClip == 1, ])   # the 2 by 4 km clip
round(cor(Z[, c("Elevation","Wind","WindResid")]), 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-orthogonality
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "How much of each candidate predictor is elevation. The wind product is a downscaled mesoscale field draped over terrain and is largely an elevation transform. The heat load and shelter indices are computed from the same elevation model by trigonometry and are almost unrelated to it. Being terrain-derived and being an elevation transform are not the same thing."

tibble(Surface = c("Global Wind Atlas wind speed", "Heat load index (McCune and Keon)",
                   "Shelter index (Winstral, omnidirectional)", "Topographic position, 625 m"),
       `How it is built` = c("mesoscale field downscaled over the DEM",
                             "trigonometric function of DEM aspect and slope",
                             "maximum upwind slope from the DEM within 500 m",
                             "deviation from surrounding DEM mean"),
       `R² on elevation` = sapply(c("Wind","HLI","SxMean","TPI600"), function(v)
         round(summary(lm(as.formula(paste(v, "~ Elevation")), data = Z))$r.squared, 3))) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llr") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)
```

## Response coding

@krawchuk2020 warn specifically against coding refugia as a binary, on the grounds that a refugium is a matter of degree and that thresholding discards the part of the signal that distinguishes a lightly touched stand from a destroyed one. The survey carries an ordinal severity class, so we can follow that advice. We fit the binary attacked model above for comparability with the refugia literature, and alongside it a cumulative logit at each severity threshold: the probability that a cell reached trace or worse, light or worse, moderate or worse, and severe or worse. Fitting the thresholds separately rather than imposing a single proportional-odds slope is deliberate. It is also the standard diagnostic for whether proportional odds holds, and @sec-ordinal shows that here it does not.

# Results

Raw attack appeared strongly unimodal. Conditioning on host presence flattens the gradient below 1,900 m, but not above it, where attack halves while lodgepole cover rises and stands thin.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gradient
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Attack across the elevation gradient, before and after conditioning on lodgepole presence. Raw attack is strongly unimodal. Conditioning on host presence flattens the gradient below 1,900 m, but not above it, where attack halves while lodgepole cover rises and stands thin."

S$band <- cut(S$Elevation, breaks = seq(500, 2400, 200), dig.lab = 5)
grad <- S |> group_by(band) |>
  summarise(Cells = n(),
            `Pine cover (%)` = round(mean(PinePct), 1),
            `Basal area` = round(mean(Basal, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            `Wind (m/s)` = round(mean(Wind), 2),
            `Attacked, all cells (%)` = round(100 * mean(Attacked), 1),
            `Attacked, host present (%)` =
              ifelse(sum(HasHost) > 300, round(100 * mean(Attacked[HasHost]), 1), NA),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(Cells > 500)
grad |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)

## Spread of host-conditioned attack below 1,900 m, quoted in the text below.
hp_low <- S |> filter(HasHost, Elevation < 1900) |>
  mutate(b = cut(Elevation, seq(500, 1900, 200))) |>
  group_by(b) |> summarise(n = n(), pct = 100 * mean(Attacked), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n > 300)
HP_RANGE <- range(hp_low$pct)

## Host cover above the threshold, compared two ways, because the two
## comparisons disagree and reporting only the flattering one would be the
## same denominator trick this paper criticises in @sec-lowtrap. PINE_LO is
## the whole gradient below the threshold, which is dominated by the pine-poor
## valley; PINE_ADJ is the 150 m band immediately below it.
PINE_HI  <- mean(H$PinePct[H$Elevation >= ALPINE])
PINE_LO  <- mean(H$PinePct[H$Elevation <  ALPINE])
PINE_ADJ <- mean(H$PinePct[H$Elevation >= ALPINE - 150 & H$Elevation < ALPINE])
```

Across the full gradient, attack is strongly unimodal (@tbl-gradient, @fig-gradient). It rises from under three per cent in the valley to a peak near 1,430 m and falls away to zero above 2,100 m.

Conditioning on host presence separates that curve into two different phenomena. Below roughly 1,900 m the hump is host distribution: among cells that contain lodgepole, attack runs between `r sprintf("%.0f", HP_RANGE[1])` and `r sprintf("%.0f", HP_RANGE[2])` per cent with no strong trend from the valley bottom upward, and the dramatic rise in the raw curve is the rise in pine cover. Attack is `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(S$Attacked[S$HasHost]))` per cent where lodgepole is present against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(S$Attacked[!S$HasHost]))` per cent where it is absent.

Above `r format(ALPINE, big.mark = ",")` m the conditioning does not remove the decline. Attack among host-bearing cells falls by about half, while stand basal area falls from `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(H$Basal[H$Elevation<ALPINE], na.rm=TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(H$Basal[H$Elevation>=ALPINE], na.rm=TRUE))`. Stands are thinner and attack is suppressed.

Host cover is the conjunct that decides whether this is the pattern the @krawchuk2020 hypothesis requires, and it depends on the comparison, so we give both. Against the whole gradient below, mean lodgepole cover in host-bearing cells is `r sprintf("%.1f", PINE_HI)` per cent above the threshold against `r sprintf("%.1f", PINE_LO)` per cent below: essentially unchanged, so host scarcity cannot account for an attack rate that more than halves. Against the `r format(ALPINE - 150, big.mark = ",")` to `r format(ALPINE, big.mark = ",")` m band immediately below, however, cover is `r sprintf("%.1f", PINE_ADJ)` per cent, so the top of the gradient does carry about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - PINE_HI / PINE_ADJ))` per cent less pine than the band beneath it. The first comparison is flattered by the pine-poor valley it includes, which is the denominator problem @sec-lowtrap is about, and we would be inconsistent to rely on it alone.

The honest reading is that host thins somewhat at the top of the gradient while attack falls a great deal more, and the conjunction the hypothesis requires holds in the weaker form: the decline in attack is far too large to be a proportionate response to the decline in host. It is not the clean case of host holding constant.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gradient
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "(a) Attack across the gradient, raw and conditioned on lodgepole presence, with mean lodgepole cover. Conditioning flattens the curve below 1,900 m and does not above it. (b) The same data against wind speed: wind rises monotonically with elevation while attack turns over, so no monotone wind relationship can hold across the gradient. Shading marks the elevation range of the 2 by 4 km clip."

fine <- S |> mutate(b = cut(Elevation, breaks = seq(500, 2350, 100))) |>
  group_by(b) |>
  summarise(el = mean(Elevation), raw = 100*mean(Attacked), pine = mean(PinePct),
            wind = mean(Wind), n = n(),
            cond = ifelse(sum(HasHost) > 150, 100*mean(Attacked[HasHost]), NA_real_),
            .groups = "drop") |> filter(n > 300)
crng <- range(S$Elevation[S$InClip == 1])

pa <- ggplot(fine) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = crng[1], xmax = crng[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#b2182b", alpha = .10) +
  geom_line(aes(el, raw,  colour = "all cells"), linewidth = .9) +
  geom_line(aes(el, cond, colour = "host present"), linewidth = .9) +
  geom_line(aes(el, pine, colour = "lodgepole cover (%)"), linetype = "22", linewidth = .8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("all cells" = "#2b4162", "host present" = "#b2182b",
                                 "lodgepole cover (%)" = "#3f8f9b"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Elevation (m)", y = "Per cent", title = "(a) The hump is host, except at the top") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

pb <- ggplot(fine, aes(wind, raw)) +
  geom_path(colour = "#3f8f9b", linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = el), size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours = c("#2b4162","#3f8f9b","#c6d8af","#e8c07d","#8c4b3c"),
                         name = "Elev (m)") +
  labs(x = "Mean wind speed (m/s)", y = "Attacked (%)",
       title = "(b) Wind is monotone, attack is not")
pa + pb
```

## The Krawchuk test {#sec-krawchuk}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-krawchuk
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The hypothesis test. Cells containing lodgepole pine only. Coefficients are per standard deviation; wind is entered as the component orthogonal to elevation. Intervals are percentile intervals from resampled 1 km spatial blocks, at the replicate count given in the Inference section. Only host cover clears the interval test; the orthogonalised wind term is the strongest negative coefficient and is directionally stable, but its interval reaches zero."

mt_h <- model_table(ZH)
fmt_model(mt_h) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrc") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: krawchuk-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
wr <- mt_h[mt_h$term == "WindResid", ]
pp <- mt_h[mt_h$term == "PinePct", ]
```

Restricted to cells that contain host, the orthogonalised wind term is the largest negative coefficient in the model, `r sprintf("%+.3f", wr$beta)` per standard deviation, comparable in magnitude to the positive effect of lodgepole cover itself at `r sprintf("%+.3f", pp$beta)` (@tbl-krawchuk). Its sign is reproduced in `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*wr$sign_stab)` per cent of spatial block resamples. Its 95 per cent block interval, however, runs `r sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", wr$lo, wr$hi)` and reaches zero.

On this fit the hypothesis is supported in direction and unresolved in magnitude, and @sec-nonlinear later withdraws even the direction, so this section should be read as the conventional analysis whose specification we go on to test rather than as a result we stand behind. The descriptive result in @sec-ordinal is not in doubt: attack more than halves at the top of the gradient while host cover thins only slightly. What is in doubt is whether the wind surface is the right explanation for it, and with roughly `r length(unique(ZH$block))` independent 1 km blocks in this landscape the binary response cannot settle it. Host cover is the only term whose interval excludes zero, and it does so in the expected direction.

That verdict is a property of the response coding rather than of the data, and @sec-ordinal revisits it. We report the binary model first because it is the form the refugia literature uses, and because the comparison between the two is itself a result.

Note also that elevation, entered alongside the orthogonalised wind term, is itself negative and unsupported. Once host is in the model the remaining elevation signal is weak; the suppression at the top of the gradient is not simply an elevation effect.

## Disturbance severity metrics {#sec-ordinal}

The orthogonalised wind coefficient strengthens monotonically as the threshold rises and its block interval excludes zero at every threshold above trace, which the binary attacked model does not show.

```{r}
#| label: polr-fit
#| echo: false
#| output: false

## Fitted only to show what a single proportional-odds summary conceals; the
## threshold-specific fits in @tbl-ordinal are the result.
zo <- ZH; zo$sev <- factor(pmin(zo$Severity, 4L), levels = 0:4, ordered = TRUE)
polr_fit <- MASS::polr(sev ~ Elevation + WindResid + PinePct + Basal +
                             TPI600 + Slope + TWI + RIX,
                       data = zo, method = "logistic", Hess = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ordinal
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Cumulative logits at each severity threshold, cells containing lodgepole pine only. Each row is the same model fitted to a harder threshold. The orthogonalised wind coefficient strengthens monotonically as the threshold rises and its block interval excludes zero at every threshold above trace, which the binary attacked model does not show."

CUTS <- tibble(k = 1:4,
               label = c("trace or worse", "light or worse",
                         "moderate or worse", "severe or worse"))

cum <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(CUTS)), function(i) {
  z <- ZH; z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= CUTS$k[i])
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z), z$y)
  bs  <- block_boot(z)
  q   <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Threshold = CUTS$label[i], Cells = sum(z$y),
         `Wind residual beta` = coef(fit)[["WindResid"]],
         lo = q[1], hi = q[2],
         `sign stability` = mean(sign(bs[, "WindResid"]) ==
                                 sign(coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]), na.rm = TRUE),
         `Pine cover beta` = coef(fit)[["PinePct"]],
         `Elevation beta`  = coef(fit)[["Elevation"]])
}) |> bind_rows()

cum |> transmute(Threshold, Cells,
                 `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", `Wind residual beta`),
                 `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", lo, hi),
                 `sign stability` = sprintf("%.2f", `sign stability`),
                 `Pine cover beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", `Pine cover beta`),
                 Supported = ifelse(lo * hi > 0, "yes", "no")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrc", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)
```

Collapsing the response to attacked or not costs the study its main result. Fitted at successively harder severity thresholds, the orthogonalised wind coefficient does not stay put: it strengthens monotonically from `r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[1])` at trace or worse to `r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[4])` at severe or worse, a `r sprintf("%.1f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[4] / cum$"Wind residual beta"[1])`-fold increase (@tbl-ordinal). At every threshold above trace the block interval excludes zero. The first row is the binary model of @sec-krawchuk restated, since a cell reaching trace or worse is exactly a cell recorded as attacked, so the table is a strict extension of that fit rather than a competing one. It is also the weakest of the four, and it is the one the refugia literature would conventionally have reported.

This is a dose-response gradient of the shape the hypothesis predicts. Wherever the wind surface has a component independent of elevation, that component is associated with less attack, and the association is strongest where attack was heaviest. It also explains the binary result: a cell that reached trace severity is barely distinguishable from an unattacked cell, so a threshold drawn between them puts most of the noise in the response exactly where the model is asked to fit.

The slopes differ by a factor of `r sprintf("%.1f", cum$"Wind residual beta"[4] / cum$"Wind residual beta"[1])` across the thresholds, so proportional odds does not hold and a single ordinal coefficient would be the wrong summary. Fitting one anyway returns `r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(polr_fit)[["WindResid"]])`, close to the trace-threshold estimate and concealing everything above it. Two other terms move with the threshold and are worth recording. Lodgepole cover, the only term that cleared the interval test in the binary model, weakens as the threshold rises and reverses at severe or worse (`r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Pine cover beta"[4])`). One reading is ecological: host abundance governs whether a stand is attacked at all, not how hard. A second is an artefact of the inventory's vintage, and we cannot separate them. As the Materials section states, composition was interpreted from 2014 photography, late in the outbreak window, so stands that lost their pine early carry a lower recorded lodgepole percentage than they did when the beetle reached them. That mechanism predicts a negative coefficient appearing specifically at the heaviest severities, which is exactly what is observed. We therefore report the reversal and decline to interpret it. Elevation turns positive at moderate or worse (`r sprintf("%+.3f", cum$"Elevation beta"[3])`), which is consistent with severe attack having been concentrated in the mid-elevation pine belt rather than at either end of the gradient.

We are nonetheless not able to attribute the gradient to wind rather than to cold, and the Discussion explains why the ordinal result does not help with that. More seriously, @sec-nonlinear shows that the sweep in this table does not survive entering elevation flexibly, so what looks here like improved statistical support is largely the unimodal elevation response returning through a predictor that was orthogonalised only against the linear part of elevation. This table should be read together with that one, and not on its own.

## Wind effects by elevation {#sec-nonlinear}

The ordinal sweep refitted with elevation entered flexibly instead of linearly, and the wind surface residualised against that same basis. Elevation explains eleven points more of the wind surface once curvature is allowed, and the orthogonalised wind coefficient loses between three fifths and seven tenths of its magnitude. No threshold clears the interval test under either flexible basis.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nonlinear
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The ordinal sweep refitted with elevation entered flexibly instead of linearly, and the wind surface residualised against that same basis. Elevation explains eleven points more of the wind surface once curvature is allowed, and the orthogonalised wind coefficient loses between three fifths and seven tenths of its magnitude. No threshold clears the interval test under either flexible basis."

## Everything above enters elevation as one linear term, and orthogonalises wind
## against that same straight line. But @fig-gradient shows the response is
## unimodal in elevation, and a straight line through a hump leaves a structured,
## elevation-shaped residual that any covariate correlated with the curvature can
## absorb. The wind surface is such a covariate by construction, because the
## downscaling is a nonlinear function of terrain. Residualising against a line
## cannot remove curvature the line never described. This table tests that.

elev_basis <- function(E, basis) switch(basis,
  linear = cbind(ElevL = E),
  quad   = cbind(ElevL = E, ElevQ = E^2),
  spline = { b <- splines::ns(E, df = 4); colnames(b) <- paste0("ElevS", 1:4); as.matrix(b) })

nl_row <- function(basis) {
  z  <- ZH
  EB <- elev_basis(z$Elevation, basis)
  z  <- cbind(z[, setdiff(names(z), "Elevation")], as.data.frame(EB))
  ## wind residualised on THIS basis, not on the straight line
  z$WindResid <- as.numeric(scale(residuals(lm(z$Wind ~ EB))))
  vars <- c(colnames(EB), "WindResid", "PinePct", "Basal", "TPI600", "Slope", "TWI", "RIX")
  r2 <- summary(lm(z$Wind ~ EB))$r.squared
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(CUTS)), function(i) {
    z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= CUTS$k[i])
    fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z, vars), z$y)
    bs  <- block_boot(z, vars)
    q   <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
    ## numeric, so the prose can compute with them; formatted only for display
    tibble(basis = basis, r2 = r2, threshold = CUTS$label[i],
           beta = coef(fit)[["WindResid"]], lo = q[1], hi = q[2])
  }) |> bind_rows()
}
nl <- bind_rows(lapply(c("linear","quad","spline"), nl_row))

## Named lookups for the prose below. The inline expressions in an executable
## manuscript are read as often as the output is, so they are kept to plain
## names, and they select on basis and threshold rather than on row position.
r2   <- function(basis) nl$r2[nl$basis == basis][1]
beta <- function(basis, thresh) nl$beta[nl$basis == basis & nl$threshold == thresh]

nl |> transmute(`Elevation basis` = basis,
                `R² wind on basis` = sprintf("%.3f", r2),
                Threshold = threshold,
                `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", beta),
                `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", lo, hi),
                Supported = ifelse(lo * hi > 0, "yes", "no")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrlrrc") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9)
```

@sandel2015 gives the diagnostic that motivates this test. For a genuinely linear relationship a coefficient is extent-independent and only the coefficient of determination moves as the extent changes; a coefficient that changes sign under truncation is therefore a symptom of an unmodelled nonlinearity rather than evidence of a general law of extent. Our response is unimodal in elevation and our wind surface is monotone in it, which is exactly the configuration that produces such a symptom, so the specification has to be tested rather than assumed.

It does not pass. Entering elevation as a quadratic raises the share of the wind surface that elevation explains from `r sprintf("%.3f", r2("linear"))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", r2("quad"))`, and a natural spline on four degrees of freedom raises it to `r sprintf("%.3f", r2("spline"))`. About `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (r2("spline") - r2("linear")))` percentage points of the wind surface's variance is therefore nonlinear in elevation, and the linear orthogonalisation used above leaves all of it inside what we had been calling the component of wind independent of elevation.

When that residue is removed the wind result goes with it. At severe or worse the coefficient falls from `r sprintf("%+.3f", beta("linear", "severe or worse"))` to `r sprintf("%+.3f", beta("quad", "severe or worse"))`, and at moderate or worse from `r sprintf("%+.3f", beta("linear", "moderate or worse"))` to `r sprintf("%+.3f", beta("quad", "moderate or worse"))`, a loss of `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - beta("quad", "severe or worse") / beta("linear", "severe or worse")))` and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - beta("quad", "moderate or worse") / beta("linear", "moderate or worse")))` per cent of magnitude respectively. Under both flexible bases every interval covers zero at every threshold. The monotone strengthening across thresholds survives in the point estimates, but nothing in the sweep clears the test this paper set itself.

We report this as the result rather than relegating it to a sensitivity appendix, because it changes what the preceding two sections mean. The dose-response in @tbl-ordinal is not evidence about wind. It is very largely the unimodal elevation response reappearing through a predictor that was never orthogonal to the curvature of elevation, only to its slope. The honest conclusion is that this study does not have a wind effect to report, and that the appearance of one was a consequence of how elevation was specified.

## Thermal load by aspect {#sec-aspect}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-aspect
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The host-present model with the two aspect-derived terms added, at each severity threshold the extended model can carry. Heat load is positive and strengthens sharply with severity: warmer aspects burn harder at the same elevation. The orthogonalised wind term is not displaced by it and in fact strengthens. The shelter index points the other way, which the text takes seriously rather than explaining away."

FULLV <- c(MODEL_VARS, EXTRA)
ZHx   <- ZH[complete.cases(ZH[, FULLV]), ]

## Ten terms and 1,522 events cannot be fitted together: the severe threshold
## drives fitted probabilities to numerical zero. We detect that rather than
## report the resulting coefficients, and the severe row is dropped below.
sep_check <- function(z, vars, k) {
  z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= k)
  p <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z, vars), z$y)$fitted.values
  sum(p < 1e-6 | p > 1 - 1e-6)
}
sep <- sapply(1:4, function(k) sep_check(ZHx, FULLV, k))
names(sep) <- c("trace+","light+","moderate+","severe+")
OK_CUTS <- which(sep == 0)

asp_tab <- lapply(OK_CUTS, function(k) {
  z <- ZHx; z$y <- as.integer(z$Severity >= k)
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z, FULLV), z$y); bs <- block_boot(z, FULLV)
  ci <- function(n) quantile(bs[, n], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  one <- function(n) sprintf("%+.3f [%+.3f, %+.3f]", coef(fit)[[n]], ci(n)[1], ci(n)[2])
  tibble(Threshold = CUTS$label[k], Cells = sum(z$y),
         `Wind residual` = one("WindResid"), `Heat load` = one("HLI"),
         `Shelter` = one("SxMean"))
}) |> bind_rows()

asp_tab |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr",
                 format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9)
```

The inherited predictor set had no aspect in it, so until now the model could not tell a warm slope from a cold one at the same elevation. Adding two aspect-derived terms does three things.

First, it supplies the one piece of thermal information available without a temperature surface. Heat load is positive at every threshold and strengthens steeply with severity (@tbl-aspect). Since heat load is essentially uncorrelated with elevation (@tbl-orthogonality), this is not the elevation gradient returning under another name: at a given elevation, southwest-facing ground carries heavier beetle-caused mortality than northeast-facing ground. That is the sign cold limitation predicts, and it is the first evidence in this study that the thermal axis is doing work independently of elevation.

Second, it leaves the wind coefficient standing. The orthogonalised wind term does not weaken when heat load is controlled for; it strengthens slightly at every threshold, so whatever the wind residual is tracking, it is not the warm-aspect effect in disguise. It is, however, largely the curvature of elevation: this model still enters elevation linearly, and @sec-nonlinear shows the wind term does not survive a flexible basis. Controlling for aspect does not rescue it.

Third, and least comfortably, the two exposure measures disagree. The shelter index is negative, meaning sheltered ground carries *less* attack and exposed ground more, which is the opposite of what the orthogonalised wind term says and the opposite of what @krawchuk2020 predict. The two are only weakly correlated with each other (`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(ZHx$WindResid, ZHx$SxMean))`), so they are not two measurements of one quantity that happen to disagree; they are measuring different things, and only one of them is a direct geometric description of exposure. We take this as evidence against treating any single surface as "wind exposure" and reporting its coefficient as though the phrase had one referent. It is also a caution against our own result: the wind residual's negative sign is not corroborated by the one predictor in this study that describes exposure geometrically rather than by downscaling.

The severe threshold is absent from @tbl-aspect because ten terms and `r sum(ZHx$Severity >= 4)` events drive the fit into quasi-separation, with `r format(sep[["severe+"]], big.mark = ",")` cells at numerically zero fitted probability. The eight-term model of @tbl-ordinal is free of this at every threshold, which is why that table retains its severe row and this one does not.

## Observed winter minima do not reach the lethal threshold {#sec-cold}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cold
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Observed winter minimum air temperatures from weather stations within 100 km, by elevation band, after excluding station-winters censored at the -20.0 °C sensor floor. Nothing in the record approaches the temperatures conventionally cited as lethal for this insect. Elevation orders the minima only weakly, which is cold-air pooling."

st <- read.csv(here("02.inputs/climate/station-winter-minima.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

## The censoring rule is applied here rather than taken on trust from the
## retrieval script. Many older British Columbia Wildfire Service sensors floor
## at exactly -20.0 C. A station-winter is unusable when its minimum sits
## exactly on that floor, because the true minimum is then unknown. A minimum
## colder than the floor shows the sensor did read past it, so readings at
## -20.0 in those winters are real measurements and the winter is kept. The
## floor is a sensor artefact of that network, so the rule does not touch the
## Environment and Climate Change Canada records.
FLOOR <- -20
st$censored <- st$network == "BCWS" &
               abs(st$min_temp_c - FLOOR) < 1e-6 &
               st$n_at_minus20 > 0
stopifnot(identical(st$censored, as.logical(st$censored_flag)))

## Isolated single-observation spikes are rejected at the observation level by
## the retrieval script, which is the only stage holding the sub-daily series a
## per-winter summary cannot carry; `min_temp_c_usable` is that de-spiked
## minimum. Everything else about the screen is visible above.
use <- st[!st$censored & !is.na(st$min_temp_c_usable), ]

use$band <- cut(use$elevation_m, c(0, 800, 1500, 2500),
                labels = c("below 800 m", "800 to 1,500 m", "above 1,500 m"))
use |> group_by(band) |>
  summarise(Stations = n_distinct(station_name), `Station-winters` = n(),
            `Coldest (°C)` = min(min_temp_c_usable),
            `Mean minimum (°C)` = round(mean(min_temp_c_usable), 1),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr") |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: cold-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
coldest  <- use[which.min(use$min_temp_c_usable), ]
hi       <- use[use$elevation_m >= 1500, ]
lowcold  <- use[use$elevation_m < 800, ]
lowcold  <- lowcold[which.min(lowcold$min_temp_c_usable), ]
```

The cold explanation for the high-elevation suppression assumes it gets cold enough up there to kill beetles. That is checkable against observation, and it does not hold. Across `r nrow(use)` station-winters from `r n_distinct(use$station_name)` stations spanning `r min(use$elevation_m)` to `r max(use$elevation_m)` m, retrieved and screened by the script in `02.inputs/climate/`, the coldest defensible winter minimum anywhere in the region is `r sprintf("%.1f", coldest$min_temp_c_usable)` °C, at `r tolower(coldest$station_name)` at `r format(round(coldest$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m in winter `r coldest$winter_year`. The number of station-winters reaching -35 °C or colder is `r sum(use$min_temp_c_usable <= -35)`, and the number reaching -40 °C or colder is `r sum(use$min_temp_c_usable <= -40)`. Above 1,500 m the mean winter minimum is `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(hi$min_temp_c_usable))` °C. The temperatures conventionally cited as lethal for mountain pine beetle larvae sit near -40 °C under bark, the figure at which @safranyik2006 report complete mortality, while @cooke2009mortality measure a larval supercooling point with a median lethal value near -37 °C and caution against treating any fixed threshold as sufficient. Both are roughly ten degrees colder than anything this record contains. We note that neither is an air temperature and that phloem tracks air closely enough, within about two degrees, that the comparison holds; and that cold mortality is graded rather than a threshold, so the margin below is a margin against substantial mortality rather than a guarantee of none.

Two features of the record matter for the argument. Elevation orders these minima only weakly: `r tolower(lowcold$station_name)`, at `r format(round(lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m, reaches `r sprintf("%.1f", lowcold$min_temp_c_usable)` °C, within `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(lowcold$min_temp_c_usable - coldest$min_temp_c_usable))` °C of the alpine station `r format(round(coldest$elevation_m - lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m higher. That is cold-air pooling, and it is the reason temperature cannot be treated as a linear function of elevation here. And `r sum(st$censored)` station-winters had to be set aside because the sensors floor at exactly -20.0 °C, a censoring artefact concentrated before 2008; taking a naive minimum over those would have manufactured a threshold that is not in the data.

This is a plausibility check and not a temperature surface. No station inside the study area reported during the outbreak window, and the stations that do report are spread across roughly 100 km of separate massifs, so these values bound the regional cold climate rather than map it. Within that limit the conclusion is reasonably firm: direct freeze mortality is unlikely to be what suppresses attack at the top of this gradient.

## Extent governs whether the coefficient is estimable at all {#sec-extent}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-extent
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The same model fitted at three extents. As the analysis area shrinks, the share of wind variance explained by elevation rises and the orthogonalised wind coefficient reverses sign. The 2 by 4 km clip is the extent at which the companion study was run and is typical of disturbance ecology generally."

extent_row <- function(z, lab) {
  r2  <- summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = z))$r.squared
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z), z$y)
  bs  <- block_boot(z)
  q   <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  ## The block count is reported because it, not the cell count, is the
  ## resampling unit. The clip holds few enough blocks that its interval is
  ## far weaker than its cell count suggests, and the reader must see that.
  tibble(Extent = lab, Cells = nrow(z), Blocks = length(unique(z$block)),
         `R² wind on elevation` = round(r2, 3),
         ## This is the variance inflation the *raw* wind term would carry
         ## against elevation. It is not the VIF of the fitted model, in which
         ## the residualised term is orthogonal to elevation by construction and
         ## its VIF is 1. It is reported to show the collinearity that
         ## orthogonalisation reparameterises away rather than removes.
         `VIF of raw wind` = round(1/(1-r2), 1),
         `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]),
         `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2]))
}
bind_rows(
  extent_row(Z,  sprintf("full landscape (%.0f km²)", nrow(S)*prod(res(G))/1e6)),
  extent_row(ZH, "landscape, host present"),
  extent_row(ZC, sprintf("2 by 4 km clip (%.1f km²)",
                         sum(S$InClip == 1) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6))
) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)
```

The confound is a function of extent, and so is the answer. Across the landscape elevation explains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = Z))$r.squared)` per cent of the variance in the wind surface; inside the 2 by 4 km clip it explains `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = ZC))$r.squared)` per cent (@tbl-extent). The orthogonalised wind coefficient is negative at landscape extent and **positive** inside the clip.

Two claims live in that table and they carry very different weight, so we separate them.

The collinearity result is firm. The share of wind variance that elevation explains rises from `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = Z))$r.squared)` across the landscape to `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = ZC))$r.squared)` inside the clip, and that quantity is a property of the two surfaces rather than an estimate with sampling error in the usual sense. It is the mechanism this paper is about, and it does not depend on resolving the Krawchuk hypothesis.

The sign reversal is a comparison of two point estimates and is not, on this evidence, a demonstrated reversal. The clip contains only `r length(unique(ZC$block))` spatial blocks, so its block interval runs `r {q <- quantile(block_boot(ZC)[, "WindResid"], c(.025,.975), na.rm = TRUE); sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2])}`: it spans zero, and it also spans both landscape estimates. By the rule this paper set itself, that the interval must exclude zero, the clip coefficient is not distinguishable from zero, from the landscape estimate, or from its own opposite. What the clip demonstrates is that shrinking the extent destroys the ability to estimate the coefficient at all, which is a weaker claim than a reversal and still a damaging one for the practice we are criticising: a study run at this extent would report a positive point estimate with an interval too wide to notice that it had learned nothing. Establishing reversal proper would need the coefficient difference tested directly, by fitting an extent-by-wind interaction on the pooled data and bootstrapping that interaction on common blocks. We have not done that here and do not claim it.

## Grain does not decide it {#sec-grain}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-grain
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "The host-present model refitted at three grains. Predictors are aggregated by mean, severity class by maximum, the topographic position neighbourhood is held near-constant in metres, and the bootstrap blocks are rescaled to stay near 1 km. Unlike extent, grain changes nothing: the collinearity, the sign and the magnitude are all stable across a four-fold change in cell size."

CONT <- c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind","PinePct","Basal")
base_stack <- c(terr[[c("Elevation","Slope","TWI","RIX","Wind")]],
                host[[c("PinePct","Basal")]], severity, in_clip)
names(base_stack) <- c(CONT, "Severity", "InClip")

## fact is the aggregation factor from the native 25 m grid.
build_grain <- function(fact) {
  b <- if (fact == 1L) base_stack else
       c(aggregate(base_stack[[CONT]], fact, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE),
         aggregate(base_stack[[c("Severity","InClip")]], fact, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE))
  Gi <- b[["Elevation"]]; rs <- res(Gi)[1]
  w  <- max(3L, as.integer(2 * floor(625 / rs / 2) + 1))   # odd window nearest 625 m
  b$TPI600 <- tpi(Gi, w)
  d <- as.data.frame(b, na.rm = FALSE)
  d$Attacked <- d$Severity > 0
  d$HasHost  <- !is.na(d$PinePct) & d$PinePct > 0
  blk <- max(1L, as.integer(round(BLOCK / fact)))          # blocks stay near 1 km
  rc  <- rowColFromCell(Gi, seq_len(ncell(Gi)))
  d$block <- paste(rc[,1] %/% blk, rc[,2] %/% blk, sep = "_")
  d <- d[complete.cases(d[, MVARS]), ]
  structure(d, res = rs, win = w * rs)
}

grain_row <- function(fact) {
  d  <- build_grain(fact); h <- d[d$HasHost, ]
  z  <- standardise(h)
  r2 <- summary(lm(Wind ~ Elevation, data = z))$r.squared
  fit <- fit_fast(design_matrix(z), z$y); bs <- block_boot(z)
  q  <- quantile(bs[, "WindResid"], c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Grain = sprintf("%.0f m", attr(d, "res")),
         `TPI window` = sprintf("%.0f m", attr(d, "win")),
         `Host cells` = nrow(h), Blocks = length(unique(z$block)),
         `R² wind on elevation` = round(r2, 3),
         `Wind residual beta` = sprintf("%+.3f", coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]),
         `block 95% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", q[1], q[2]),
         `sign stability` = sprintf("%.2f",
           mean(sign(bs[, "WindResid"]) == sign(coef(fit)[["WindResid"]]), na.rm = TRUE)))
}

## The 25 m row must reproduce the analysis frame built in `assemble`; if this
## assertion ever fails the two code paths have drifted apart.
stopifnot(nrow(build_grain(1L)) == nrow(S))

bind_rows(lapply(c(1L, 2L, 4L), grain_row)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrrrr", format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)
```

@work2011, working on carabid beetles, found that the apparent importance of terrain derivatives changed with the resolution at which they were computed, because elevation error propagates into derived curvature differently at every grain. The concern transfers directly and is worth separating from extent, because the two are routinely confused.

Here they behave quite differently (@tbl-grain). Aggregating the analysis from 25 m to 100 m, a sixteen-fold reduction in the number of cells, leaves the confound essentially untouched: elevation explains close to the same share of wind variance at every grain. The orthogonalised wind coefficient neither reverses nor decays, and its sign stability rises rather than falls. The suppression at the top of the gradient is a landscape-scale feature and it survives being looked at through a coarser lens.

The contrast with @sec-extent is the point, and it is a contrast we should be careful not to overstate. Enlarging the cell by a factor of four changes almost nothing here; shrinking the study area destroys the estimate. Grain governs how finely a pattern is resolved, extent governs which part of the joint distribution of elevation and wind the model ever sees, and in this study only the second mattered.

That is a result about this landscape and this pair of surfaces, not a general ordering of the two axes. @wiens1989 set out the distinction and warned in the same paper that correlations evident within one domain may disappear or change sign when the extent is enlarged past it, and @dungan2002 had already recommended that studies report unit size, shape, spacing and extent together for exactly this reason. The literature since has not settled which axis matters more, and where it has looked it has often found the opposite of what we find: @mcgarigal2016, reviewing several hundred multi-scale habitat studies, concluded that the emphasis on extent may if anything have left grain under-examined. Nor is reporting the weak point we first assumed. @estes2018 audited the ecological literature and found resolution and extent reported at closely comparable rates, near three fifths in both cases, so there is no asymmetry to correct.

What our result does add is narrower and we think more useful. @sandel2015 shows that for a genuinely linear relationship the coefficient is extent-independent and only the coefficient of determination moves with extent. A coefficient that changes sign under truncation is therefore a diagnostic for an unmodelled nonlinearity rather than an instance of a general law. That is very likely what is happening here, and this paper contains the evidence for it: @fig-gradient shows attack unimodal in elevation while wind rises monotonically, so no monotone wind term can hold across the whole gradient, and the clip lands on one limb of the hump. Read that way the finding is not "extent reverses inferences" but the sharper and more testable "truncating a gradient onto one limb of a unimodal response will reverse the apparent sign of anything monotonically correlated with the gradient." Testing it properly means fitting the nonlinearity rather than assuming it away, which this study does not do and which is the first thing we would do next.

# Discussion

## Constraints to terrain-wind predictors of refugia 

The high-elevation suppression is real and it is not host limitation. Among cells carrying lodgepole pine, attack above `r format(ALPINE, big.mark=",")` m runs at `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(H$Attacked[H$Elevation>=ALPINE]))` per cent against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100*mean(H$Attacked[H$Elevation<ALPINE]))` per cent below, while mean pine cover in those cells is `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*(1 - PINE_HI/PINE_ADJ))` per cent lower than in the band immediately below and basal area is roughly a fifth lower, so the fall in attack is several times larger than the fall in host. Under the @krawchuk2020 definition these are refugia: locations disturbed less severely than the surrounding landscape, with host present, and predictably located by an enduring topographic feature. They match @cartwright2018 in associating refugia with thinner stands.

What we cannot do is attribute them to wind, and it is worth being precise about why, because the ordinal result in @sec-ordinal changes one half of the difficulty and leaves the other exactly where it was.

The statistical half looked, at first, much improved. Once severity is modelled as the ordinal variable it is, the orthogonalised wind term clears the interval test at every threshold above trace and strengthens monotonically with severity, and on that basis we initially took the binary null to be an artefact of coding. @sec-nonlinear withdraws that reading. Entering elevation flexibly, and residualising the wind surface against the same flexible basis rather than against a straight line, removes between three fifths and seven tenths of the coefficient and leaves no threshold clearing the interval test. The ordinal coding does recover structure the binary discards, and @krawchuk2020's conceptual warning against binary refugia coding stands. But the structure it recovers is not, on this evidence, attributable to wind: it is very largely the curvature of the elevation response, which the linear specification pushed into the wind term. We therefore do not report a wind effect, in either coding.

The identification half is untouched. The upper gradient is also where it is coldest, and cold limits this beetle through overwinter mortality and through the degree-day accumulation required for univoltine development [@carroll2004bionomics; @cooke2009mortality; @safranyik2006]. Crucially, cold predicts a dose-response in severity just as wind disruption does: fewer beetles surviving the winter means both fewer stands attacked and lighter attack in those that are. The monotone strengthening across thresholds is therefore fully consistent with cold limitation and does nothing to separate the two. Orthogonalising against elevation removes the linear elevation component of the wind surface, but it does not orthogonalise against temperature, which is not a linear function of elevation in a landscape with cold-air pooling.

We looked for a way out and do not think one exists at this extent. Separating exposure from cold needs a temperature surface whose fine-scale structure is not itself a function of the elevation model, and any surface of the form intercept plus lapse rate times elevation is an affine rescaling of the elevation layer no matter whether the lapse rate came from a physical constant or from real thermometers. It is collinear by construction and contributes nothing the elevation term does not already carry. Only a residual departure from that form would identify anything, and mapping such a residual across this landscape would itself require terrain as the interpolator. The gridded products with genuine sub-kilometre temperature structure all obtain it by regression or lapse rate onto a digital elevation model, so they reproduce the problem rather than solve it, and satellite land surface temperature is a nighttime and cloud-limited observation whose topographic correction in rugged terrain takes a high-resolution elevation model as an input.

Two results narrow the problem without dissolving it, and they work together.

The first is that cold limitation here is almost certainly not freeze mortality. @sec-cold shows that observed winter minima across the region fall roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(-40 - coldest$min_temp_c_usable))` degrees short of the temperatures conventionally cited as lethal for this insect, at every elevation for which there is a record. If larvae are not being killed outright, the cold mechanism that remains is the degree-day accumulation required to complete a generation in one year, which is a matter of accumulated warmth rather than of extreme events.

The second is that aspect gives purchase on exactly that. Because heat load is a trigonometric function of the elevation model rather than a field draped over it, it carries thermal information genuinely independent of elevation, and @sec-aspect finds it predicts attack severity strongly and in the direction warmth-limited development implies. The two results therefore point the same way: the thermal constraint that plausibly operates on this landscape is the one for which we have an elevation-independent proxy, and that proxy behaves as the constraint predicts.

This is a real gain and it is bounded in three ways. The station record is a regional plausibility check and not a temperature surface, since no station inside the study area reported during the outbreak window. Heat load is a modelled radiation load, not a measured temperature. And neither result touches the possibility that cold-air pooling produces local freeze events the regional station network never sampled, which is precisely the structure @sec-cold shows is present when a valley station at `r format(round(lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m matches an alpine station `r format(round(coldest$elevation_m - lowcold$elevation_m), big.mark=",")` m above it.

The deeper obstacle is that the quantity governing overwinter survival is not air temperature at all but temperature under the bark, which is not observed at landscape scale anywhere. @goodsman2024, validating the standard Canadian Forest Service winter mortality model against observed mortality in Banff National Park, found its spatial predictions poor and attributed the failure to precisely this: mountainous terrain is a hard prediction problem when under-bark temperatures are not measured directly. That is peer-reviewed confirmation that the confound we report unresolved is unresolved in this terrain generally, and not an artefact of our data being thin.

There is also a class of mechanism that would produce our result without involving pheromone plumes at all, and it should not be waved past. If exposed ground receives fewer arriving beetles, rather than the same number arriving to a disrupted signal, the observable consequence in a static model is identical: less attack on exposed convexities. We advance that as an alternative hypothesis of our own rather than as a finding transferred from elsewhere, because the obvious precedent does not in fact support it. @smithmckenna2013, working on white pine blister rust in whitebark pine treeline communities, established that topographic position governs the delivery of a wind-borne propagule, which is the general premise the alternative needs; but the direction they report is the opposite of the one it would require, with high and exposed positions favouring *interception* of wind-dispersed spores rather than escaping it. Their agent is a fungus and its transport is passive rather than behavioural, so neither direction transfers cleanly to a flying insect that selects where it lands. What their result does establish is that the dispersal pathway is a live confound in terrain of this kind, whichever sign it takes here. Nothing in our design distinguishes it from pheromone disruption. Distinguishing them would need the dispersal process observed rather than inferred, through attack years, distance from the previous year's attack, or trapping.

The honest summary is that we have located candidate refugia, confirmed the host-density half of the hypothesis, and found the wind half statistically well supported once severity is modelled properly, but still confounded with at least two alternative explanations on the same gradient.

## The low-elevation trap {#sec-lowtrap}

The result that should travel furthest is the one at the bottom of the gradient. Attack there is near zero, and any refugia mapping exercise that lacked a host layer would have identified the valley as a large, spatially coherent, topographically predictable refugium. It is not a refugium. It is a place with almost no pine. Conditioning on host raises attack in the lowest band from `r sprintf("%.1f", grad$"Attacked, all cells (%)"[1])` per cent to `r sprintf("%.1f", grad$"Attacked, host present (%)"[1])` per cent, which is within the range observed at mid elevations.

@krawchuk2020 anticipate this in framing, asking of any candidate refugium both what it is a refugium from and what it is a refugium for, but the framework does not force the check and the data required to perform it are not always at hand. On this landscape the difference between performing it and not is the difference between reporting a `r sprintf("%.0f", sum(S$Elevation < 900) * prod(res(G)) / 1e6)` km2 valley refugium and reporting none. We would put the requirement more strongly than the framework currently does: a refugium claim without an independent host or habitat layer is not interpretable.

## Extent, and the transferability of terrain-derived predictors

The collinearity result in @sec-extent generalises beyond wind. The mechanism is that a fine-resolution climate surface is produced by imposing terrain on a coarse field, so wherever the coarse field is nearly constant the product approaches a function of the terrain. That covers most gridded climate products used in landscape ecology. Three properties govern the severity and all three are checkable before any model is fitted: the ratio of analysis extent to the correlation length of the driving field, the relief of the study area, and which terrain variable does the work in the downscaling, which for wind is elevation and roughness but for radiation would be slope and aspect.

The consequence for synthesis is uncomfortable. If the strength of a confound scales with study extent, effect sizes for derived climate predictors are not comparable across studies of different extents, and small studies will systematically report the strongest apparent effects. That is a pattern easily mistaken for publication bias.

We would ask three things of any study entering such a surface into a disturbance model: report its regression on elevation, report the same diagnostic at more than one extent, and interpret only the orthogonalised coefficient. None requires new data. In this study each of them changed the answer.

## Limitations

The plot record calibrates severity but not location, because coordinates for the 28 ground plots were not recoverable from the project archive. The survey response is observer sketch-mapping with known positional and severity error, and rasterising polygons imposes a grain coarser than the 25 m analysis cell; the severity classes in particular are assigned by eye from an aircraft, so the ordinal gradient in @sec-ordinal rests on an observer's judgement of proportion killed rather than on measurement. The inventory is a modelled operational product, not a census, and its species percentages are polygon-level attributes applied uniformly within polygons.
