The grain test in @sec-grain spans 25 m to 100 m, which brackets the resolutions in common use and the 900 m2 Landsat grain at which @krawchuk2020 note refugia have typically been described, but it cannot speak to behaviour at the scale of the Landsat and Sentinel products a follow-up would likely use. Finally the analysis is correlational and the outbreak is one epidemic passage; frequency refugia in the sense of @krawchuk2020 cannot be addressed with a single outbreak window, and the static design cannot separate a wind effect on pheromone communication from a wind effect on dispersal itself.

The identification gained in @sec-aspect is partial in a specific and limiting sense. Heat load bears on the degree-day accumulation half of cold limitation, the half that governs whether a generation completes in one year. It says almost nothing about the overwinter minimum half, the lethal cold events that kill larvae outright, because those are driven by synoptic air mass intrusions and cold-air pooling rather than by radiation on a slope. A model that separates warm aspects from cool ones at the same elevation has therefore addressed one of the two thermal mechanisms and left the other untouched, and the separation rests on an assumed functional form, the @mccune2002 equation, rather than on an independent measurement. Testing the overwinter half still requires temperature data this landscape does not have.

The shelter index is also imperfect as a test of the mechanism. It is omnidirectional because the Global Wind Atlas supplies no wind direction, and an omnidirectional shelter index cannot represent a process that depends on where the wind actually comes from. A directional index computed on a known prevailing bearing would be a sharper instrument, and its disagreement with the wind residual might resolve in either direction under one.

# Conclusions

Beetle-caused mortality at Darkwoods is unimodal across the \~`1,300` m of relief the modelled area spans. Below 1,900 m that pattern is the distribution of lodgepole pine, and conditioning on host removes almost all of it. Above 1,900 m it is not: attack more than halves while host cover thins only slightly and stands thin, so the decline in attack is far larger than a proportionate response to the decline in host. That is where the Krawchuk refugia hypothesis predicts refugia should be.

We do not find a wind effect. The component of the Global Wind Atlas surface orthogonal to a linear elevation term is the strongest negative predictor of attack in host-bearing stands, and modelled as the ordinal severity class it clears the interval test at every threshold above trace. But the response is unimodal in elevation, and orthogonalising against a straight line leaves the curvature of elevation inside the wind term. Entering elevation as a quadratic or a spline, and residualising wind against that same basis, collapses the coefficient at every threshold and leaves none of them clearing the test. The apparent wind signal is a specification artefact. Even had it survived, the attribution would have remained open, because cold limitation and dispersal interception both predict the same gradient; the specification result makes that question moot for this dataset.

Two further results narrow that gap without closing it. Observed winter minima from every station within 100 km fall about ten degrees short of the temperatures conventionally cited as lethal for this insect, so the cold mechanism that plausibly operates here is the accumulated warmth a generation needs, not freeze mortality. And a heat load index, which is a trigonometric function of the elevation model and therefore almost unrelated to elevation itself, predicts attack at the moderate severity threshold in the direction cold limitation implies, though not at the two lighter thresholds, so the thermal axis is doing work that is not the elevation gradient under another name. The wind residual survives its inclusion. But a geometric shelter index computed from the same elevation model carries the opposite sign to the wind residual while being nearly uncorrelated with it, which is a warning that "wind exposure" is not one measurable thing and that our own wind result lacks corroboration from the one predictor that describes exposure directly.

The methodological findings are firmer, and all three are failures of design rather than of data. Fitted inside a 2 by 4 km clip of the same landscape, elevation explains four fifths of the variance in the wind surface rather than two thirds, the wind coefficient's point estimate turns positive, and its interval widens until it excludes nothing at all; a four-fold change of grain moves none of this. Extent is the axis that governs whether the coefficient can be estimated here. We do not generalise that ordering: the most likely reading, following @sandel2015, is that truncating a gradient onto one limb of a unimodal response reverses the apparent sign of anything monotonically correlated with it, which is a statement about functional form rather than about extent as such. Collapsing severity to attacked or not converts the study's clearest relationship into a null. And without a host layer, the pine-poor valley floor would have been mapped as the largest refugium on the mountain.
